title: Project Proposal
text:
The rapid expansion of financial technology platforms has generated large volumes of customer data, creating opportunities to better understand user behaviour and financial engagement. Effectively analysing this data is essential for identifying patterns in customer usage, preferences, and interactions with financial services.
This project is motivated by the need to translate complex customer data into meaningful and accessible visualisations and insights. By exploring demographic characteristics, financial activity, and service usage, we will uncover key trends and differences across customer groups.
Additionally, we will emphasise the importance of interactive analytical tools in making data exploration more intuitive. By enabling users to dynamically explore and interpret data, we will support deeper understanding and more informed decision-making.

title: Project Proposal
text:
4.1 Exploratory Data Analysis
For this project, EDA will be conducted primarily through visualisation techniques to enable users to derive insights through interactive visual analytics. The availability of demographic, financial, behavioural, and engagement-related variables provides a multi-dimensional view of fintech customer behaviour.
We will explore variable distributions, compare customer segments, and identify patterns across variables. These exploratory insights will guide both the confirmatory analysis and the design of the Shiny application.

title: Project Proposal
text:
4.2 Confirmatory Data Analysis
For this project, CDA will be conducted in two main components.
First, we will perform hypothesis testing to assess the statistical significance of relationships and differences between variables. This includes tests such as t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square tests, and their non-parametric equivalents where appropriate.
Second, we will conduct segmentation analysis using clustering techniques to identify distinct customer groups based on their demographics, transactional behaviours, product usage, satisfaction, and location (city)-based patterns. This will provide deeper insights into the underlying structure of the dataset.
Together, these methods will ensure that key findings are statistically supported and analytically robust.

title: Project Proposal
text:
4.3 Segmentation Analysis
To ensure both statistical rigor and computational efficiency, the module employs two primary clustering algorithms tailored to different data types:

K-Means Clustering: Utilized for Transactional, and Satisfaction data. Since these metrics are purely numeric (e.g., transaction volume, NPS scores), K-Means provides a fast, scalable way to define segments based on Euclidean distance.
CLARA (Clustering Large Applications): Utilized for Demographic and Product Usage data. Because these datasets contain “mixed” data (e.g., age vs. categorical occupations), we employ the CLARA algorithm with Gower Distance. This approach is specifically optimized for large datasets, preventing memory crashes while accurately handling categorical variables.

title: Project Proposal
text:
5.1 Variable Distribution Analysis (Univariate Analysis)
This module will focus on understanding the distribution and characteristics of individual variables using exploratory data analysis (EDA). As there are no predefined benchmarks, confirmatory analysis will not be applicable.
The analysis will be structured into key categories:

Demographics: We will use bar charts for categorical variables and histograms/boxplots for numerical variables to understand the composition of the customer base.
Transaction Behaviour: We will use histograms, density plots, and boxplots to examine distributions, along with bar charts for categorical variables such as transaction type.
Product Ownership & App Usage: We will use bar charts to analyse adoption of financial products and platform engagement features.
Customer Satisfaction: We will use histograms and boxplots for numerical metrics, and bar charts for sentiment-related variables.
Text Analysis: We will preprocess text data (e.g., feature requests, complaint topics) and use bar charts to highlight the most frequent themes.

title: Project Proposal
text:
5.2 Comparative Analysis (Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis)
This module will examine relationships between variables using both visual and statistical techniques.

Categorical vs Numerical: We will use boxplots, violin/raincloud plots, and ridgeline plots to compare distributions across groups. Statistical tests (e.g., ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis) will be applied to assess significance.
Numerical vs Numerical: We will use scatter plots with trend lines to visualise relationships, supported by correlation-based analysis.
Categorical vs Categorical: We will use stacked bar charts and mosaic plots to examine associations, with chi-square tests applied for validation.
Multivariate Overview: We will use a correlation matrix to provide a summary of relationships across multiple numerical variables.

title: Project Proposal
text:
5.3 Segmentation Analysis
The module allows users to explore five specific dimensions of the Colombian market:

Demographics: Segmenting by age, occupation, and household size.
Behavioral & Transactional: Identifying “Power Users” vs. “Occasional Users” based on transaction frequency and credit utilization.
Product Usage: Grouping customers by their specific mix of credit cards, savings accounts, and insurance products.
Satisfaction & Engagement: Isolating segments with low sentiment or high support ticket ratios to identify churn risks.
Location-Based Personas: A hybrid approach using K-Means combined with Treemap visualizations to show how specific personas (e.g., “Young Digitals” or “High-Value Seniors”) are distributed across major cities like Bogotá, Medellín, and Cali.

It also includes real-time model quality metrics. Users can adjust the number of clusters and variables via the Shiny interface, immediately receiving feedback through:

AIC/BIC Scores: For evaluating model fit in numeric clusters.
Silhouette Width & Entropy: To measure the stability and separation of demographic and geographic segments.

title: Segmentation/Clustering
text:
1 Overview
The Clustering module segments customers into meaningful groups based on demographics, transaction behaviours, product usage, satisfaction, and location (city)-based patterns, enabling analysts to uncover how these factors shape financial behaviour in Colombia.
It provides an interactive environment where users can choose clustering type, variables, and number of cluster, and immediately visualize the resulting segments. It also displays cluster plots and quality metrics (AIC, BIC, likelihood ratio, entropy) to support evidence‑based selection of the “best” segmentation.


2 Packages Required








Package
Purpose
Justification for Shiny/CRAN




tidyverse
Data manipulation
Essential for the reactive data flows in Shiny.


factoextra
Visualization
Best-in-class for PCA-based cluster plots and Elbow/Silhouette methods.


cluster
Clustering: clara() algorithm
Critical: Unlike pam(), clara() is optimized for >40k rows, avoiding memory crashes.


fpc
Validation
Used to calculate Entropy and cluster stability.


treemap
Static Hierarchical View
Allows for a “nested” look at how behavioral clusters sit within Planning Regions/Locations.





Show the code
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, cluster, factoextra, fpc, treemap, ggplot2)
df <- read_csv("COFINFAD_LAB/data/cleaned_data.csv")




3 Demographic Clustering
Demographic segmentation uses CLARA (Clustering Large Applications), which is well-suited for mixed-type variables including categorical data such as gender, occupation, and marital status. CLARA works by repeatedly sampling subsets of the data and applying PAM (Partitioning Around Medoids) clustering, making it more robust to outliers than k-means.
Four plots are provided:

Cluster Plot — PCA projection of all customers coloured by cluster, showing how well-separated the demographic groups are in 2D space
Cluster Composition — proportion of customers in each cluster, helping assess whether the segmentation produces balanced or skewed groups
Within-Cluster Profiles — centroid heatmap showing the mean encoded value of each demographic variable per cluster, revealing which variables drive the differences between group.
Cluster Evaluation — silhouette plot showing how well each customer fits their assigned cluster

Since CLARA is used, cluster quality is assessed using silhouette width (higher is better, max = 1) and entropy (lower is better).

Cluster PlotCluster CompositionWithin-Cluster ProfilesSilhouette Plot




Show the code
demo_data <- df[, c("age", "gender", "occupation", "income_bracket", "education_level", "marital_status", "household_size")] 

set.seed(123)
demo_res <- clara(demo_data, k = 4, samples = 50, pamLike = TRUE) 

fviz_cluster(demo_res, geom = "point", pointsize = 1, main = "Demographic Segments") 











Show the code
# Calculate Silhouette Width 
avg_sil_demo <- demo_res$silinfo$avg.width
print(paste("Silhouette Width:",avg_sil_demo))


[1] "Silhouette Width: 0.435409065193502"






Show the code
cluster_sizes <- table(demo_res$clustering)
cluster_df <- data.frame(
  Cluster = names(cluster_sizes),
  Count   = as.numeric(cluster_sizes)
)

ggplot(cluster_df, aes(x = Cluster, y = Count, fill = Cluster)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Cluster Composition (Demographic Segments)",
       x = "Cluster",
       y = "Number of Customers") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")













Show the code
# Encode categoricals + keep only numeric columns for analysis
data_encoded <- demo_data %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ as.numeric(factor(.x)))) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.factor),    ~ as.numeric(.x))) %>%
  # Select only numeric columns (exclude customer_id, dates, etc.)
  select(where(is.numeric))

# Use your clustering result (change this line as needed)
clusters <- demo_res$clustering  # or usage_res$clustering, or sat_km$cluster

# Create heatmap - now safe!
data.frame(cluster = factor(clusters), data_encoded) %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), mean), .groups = "drop") %>%
  # Optional: select specific variables (uncomment if you want subset)
  # select(cluster, active_products, app_logins_frequency, feature_usage_diversity) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cluster, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  mutate(value_scaled = scale(value)[,1]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = variable, y = cluster, fill = value_scaled)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 2)), size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "tomato", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(title = "Cluster Centroid Heatmap (Numeric Variables Only)", 
       x = NULL, 
       y = "Cluster", 
       fill = "Scaled\\nMean") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8))













Show the code
sil <- silhouette(demo_res)

library(factoextra)
fviz_silhouette(sil,
                main = "Silhouette Plot") +
  theme_minimal()


  cluster size ave.sil.width
1       1   11          0.42
2       2   10          0.40
3       3    8          0.56
4       4   19          0.41














4 Behavioural and Transactional Clustering
Transactional segmentation uses k-means clustering on six standardised numerical variables: transaction count, average transaction value, total transaction volume, average daily transactions, weekend transaction ratio, and international transactions. All variables are scaled prior to clustering to ensure no single variable dominates due to differences in magnitude.
Five plots are provided:

Cluster Plot — PCA projection showing cluster separation across transaction dimensions
Cluster Composition — proportion of customers per cluster, highlighting dominant and niche segments
Within-Cluster Profiles — heatmap of scaled cluster centroids, identifying key behavioural differentiators such as transaction value and weekend activity
Elbow Plot — shows total within-cluster sum of squares (WSS) across k=1 to 10, helping identify the optimal number of clusters
Silhouette Plot — evaluates how well each customer fits their assigned cluster

All three metrics are available: silhouette width, entropy, and AIC/BIC. AIC and BIC penalise model complexity — lower values indicate a better balance between fit and the number of clusters chosen.

Cluster PlotCluster CompositionWithin-Cluster ProfilesElbow PlotSilhouette Plot




Show the code
trans_vars <- c("tx_count", "avg_tx_value", "total_tx_volume", "avg_daily_transactions", 
            "weekend_transaction_ratio", "international_transactions") 

trans_data <- na.omit(df[, trans_vars])
trans_scaled <- scale(trans_data)

set.seed(123)
trans_km <- kmeans(trans_scaled, centers = 5, nstart = 25) 

fviz_cluster(trans_km, data = trans_scaled, ellipse.type = "norm", main = "Behavioral Segments") 











Show the code
# Calculating AIC, BIC, Entropy, and Silhouette Width
k_trans <- nrow(trans_km$centers)
n_trans <- nrow(trans_scaled)

aic_trans <- trans_km$tot.withinss + 2 * k_trans * ncol(trans_scaled)
bic_trans <- trans_km$tot.withinss + log(n_trans) * k_trans * ncol(trans_scaled)

print(paste("AIC:", aic_trans, " | ", "BIC:", bic_trans))


[1] "AIC: 147455.984177087  |  BIC: 147719.801371392"

  Cluster = factor(trans_km$cluster),
  Count   = 1
)

# Bar plot of cluster proportions

  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), vjust = -0.5) +

       x = "Cluster",

  # select(cluster, active_products, app_logins_frequency, feature_usage_diversity) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cluster, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  mutate(value_scaled = scale(value)[,1]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = variable, y = cluster, fill = value_scaled)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 2)), size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "tomato", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(title = "Cluster Centroid Heatmap (Numeric Variables Only)", 
       x = NULL, 
       y = "Cluster", 
       fill = "Scaled\\nMean") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8))













Show the code
# Elbow plot for k = 1 to 10
k.max <- 10
k.values <- 1:k.max
wss <- sapply(k.values, function(k) {
  kmeans(trans_scaled, centers = k, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss
})

elbow_df <- data.frame(k = k.values, wss = wss)

  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +

5 Product Usage Clustering
Product usage segmentation uses CLARA clustering on five variables capturing digital engagement: active products, app login frequency, feature usage diversity, bill payment usage, and auto savings enabled. CLARA is chosen here due to the presence of binary variables (bill_payment_user, auto_savings_enabled) which are not well-suited to k-means distance calculations.
Four plots are provided:

Cluster Plot — PCA projection of usage patterns coloured by cluster
Cluster Composition — distribution of customers across clusters
Within-Cluster Profiles — heatmap highlighting which usage variables differ most across segments, particularly app login frequency
Cluster Evaluation — silhouette plot assessing cluster cohesion

AIC/BIC are shown as N/A since CLARA is used. This segmentation produces the strongest cluster structure of all four dimensions (silhouette = 0.50), suggesting that digital engagement patterns are the most reliable basis for customer differentiation.

Cluster PlotCluster CompositionWithin-Cluster ProfilesSilhouette Plot

6 Satisfaction and Engagement Clustering
Satisfaction segmentation uses k-means clustering on five standardised satisfaction variables: overall satisfaction score, base satisfaction, transaction satisfaction, product satisfaction, and app store rating. Variables are scaled prior to clustering.
Five plots are provided:

Cluster Plot — PCA projection showing how satisfaction profiles separate in 2D space
Cluster Composition — proportion of customers per cluster
Within-Cluster Profiles — heatmap of cluster centroids, showing which satisfaction dimensions vary most across groups
Elbow Plot — helps determine the optimal k; a gradual curve with no clear elbow suggests satisfaction data lacks strong natural cluster structure
Silhouette Plot — evaluates cluster fit for each customer

All three metrics are available. This segmentation produces the weakest structure (silhouette = 0.21), indicating that customers tend to rate satisfaction dimensions similarly regardless of their segment. A lower k (k=2 or k=3) may yield more interpretable results for this dimension.

7 Location-based Clustering
To obtain the clusters for Location-based Transaction behaviour, K-means + Treemap is used.

Purely numeric features: Transaction volume/counts/login frequency work perfectly with Euclidean distance (no categorical variables like demographics).
Scalability: Handles 48k rows efficiently for real-time Shiny reactivity.
Interpretable segments: Produces clean behavioral groups (high-spenders, frequent users, etc.) before geographic mapping.
Geographic discovery: Treemaps excel at showing hierarchical patterns—e.g., “Young Digital” customers dominate Bogotá while “High-Value Seniors” concentrate in Medellín.
No dendrogram needed: Unlike pure hierarchical clustering of cities, this reveals customer distribution patterns across locations rather than city-to-city similarity.



Show the code
cluster_data <- df %>%
  select(customer_id, total_tx_volume, tx_count, app_logins_frequency) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(across(-customer_id, scale)) 

set.seed(123)
kmeans_result <- kmeans(cluster_data[,-1], centers = 4) #input$k_clusters
cluster_data$segment_id <- as.factor(kmeans_result$cluster)

final_df <- df %>%
  inner_join(select(cluster_data, customer_id, segment_id), by = "customer_id")

segment_summary <- final_df %>%
  group_by(segment_id) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_age = round(mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    # Finding the most frequent income bracket
    top_income = names(sort(table(income_bracket), decreasing = TRUE))[1],
    avg_vol = round(mean(total_tx_volume, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
  ) %>%
  
  mutate(persona = case_when(
    segment_id == 1 ~ "Young Digital",
    segment_id == 2 ~ "Affluent Professional",
    segment_id == 3 ~ "Mass Market",
    segment_id == 4 ~ "High-Value Senior",
    TRUE ~ as.character(segment_id)
  ))

tree_prep_labeled <- final_df %>%
  group_by(location, segment_id) %>%
  summarise(total_vol = sum(total_tx_volume, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  left_join(segment_summary, by = "segment_id") %>%
  mutate(label_text = paste0(persona, "\nAvg Age: ", avg_age))

treemap(tree_prep_labeled,
        index = c("location", "label_text"), 
        vSize = "total_vol",
        vColor = "location",
        type = "index",
        title = "Geographic Segments by Persona & Age (CONFIFAD)",
        palette = "Set3",
        fontsize.labels = c(15, 8),          
        fontcolor.labels = c("black", "darkslategrey"),
        border.col = c("black", "white"),
        border.lwds = c(4, 1),
        align.labels = list(c("center", "center"), c("left", "top"))) #output$treemap

title: Variable Distribution Analysis
text:
1 Overview
This module focuses on understanding the distribution and characteristics of individual variables using exploratory data analysis (EDA). As there are no predefined benchmarks, confirmatory analysis will not be applicable.


2 Packages Required







Package
Reason for selection




tidyverse
Selected as the core package for data manipulation, cleaning, and visualisation (dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr)





Show the code
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, ggplot2)
df <- read_csv("COFINFAD_LAB/data/cleaned_data.csv")




3 Demographics
This section examines the distribution of demographic variables that describe the characteristics of the customer base. The variables include age, gender, location, income_bracket, education_level, marital_status, occupation, and household_size.
We use bar charts for categorical variables to understand the composition of the customer base.


Show the code
gender_counts <- df %>%
  count(gender)

ggplot(gender_counts, aes(x = gender, y = n)) + 
  geom_col(fill = "#3498db") + 
  geom_text(aes(label = n),
            vjust = -0.3) +
  labs(x = "Gender", y = "Number of Customers") +
  theme_minimal()











4 Transaction Behaviour
This section explores variables related to customer financial activity. Key variables include tx_count, avg_tx_value, total_tx_volume, preferred_transaction_type, avg_daily_transactions, and weekend_transaction_ratio.
We use histograms to examine distributions, along with bar charts for categorical variables such as transaction type.

HistogramBar Chart

5 Product Ownership
This section analyses the distribution of financial products held by customers. Relevant variables include savings_account, credit_card, personal_loan, investment_account, insurance_product, and active_products.
We use bar charts to analyse adoption of financial products.

6 App Usage and Engagement
This section examines variables related to customer interaction with the digital platform. These include app_logins_frequency, feature_usage_diversity, bill_payment_user, auto_savings_enabled.
We use bar charts to analyse platform engagement features.

title: Comparative Analysis
text:
1 Overview
This module examines relationships between variables using both visual and statistical techniques.

Categorical vs Numerical: We use boxplots, violin/raincloud plots, and ridgeline plots to compare distributions across groups. Statistical tests (e.g., ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis) will be applied to assess significance.
Numerical vs Numerical: We use scatter plots with trend lines to visualise relationships, supported by correlation-based analysis.
Categorical vs Categorical: We use stacked bar charts and mosaic plots to examine associations, with chi-square tests applied for validation.
Multivariate Overview: We use a correlation matrix to provide a summary of relationships across multiple numerical variables.



2 Packages Required







Package
Reason for selection




tidyverse
Selected as the core package for data manipulation, cleaning, and visualisation (dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr)


ggstatsplot
Selected because it automatically integrates statistical tests, effect sizes, and confidence intervals into visualisations, reducing the need for separate statistical coding.


ggdist
Selected for advanced distribution visualisations such as raincloud plots and half-eye plots.


ggridges
Selected for visualising ridge plots to visualise distributions across multiple groups


ggmosaic
Selected for visualising mosaic plots for categorical vs categorical relationships


corrplot
Selected for visualising correlation plot between multiple variables





Show the code
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, ggstatsplot, ggdist, ggridges, ggmosaic, corrplot)
df <- read_csv("COFINFAD_LAB/data/cleaned_data.csv")




3 Categorical vs Numerical Variables
This section compare the values of a numeric variable across the categories of another variable.
For example, average transaction value can be compared across income brackets to observe whether higher-income customers tend to perform higher-value transactions. Visualisations such as raincloud plots, violin plots, or boxplots are used to illustrate the distribution of values across categories. Ridgeline plots are also quite useful when the categories are many, for e.g. location.

Box PlotViolin PlotRaincloud PlotRidgeline Plot




Show the code
ggplot(df, aes(x = income_bracket, y = active_products)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#9e68aa", outliers = FALSE) +
  coord_flip()













Show the code
ggplot(df, aes(x = income_bracket, y = app_logins_frequency)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "#25238d") +
  coord_flip()













Show the code
ggplot(df, aes(x = income_bracket, y = avg_tx_value)) +  
     stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 1.5) +
  coord_flip()













Show the code
ggplot(df,
       aes(x = avg_tx_value, 
           y = location
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  theme_ridges()














4 Numerical vs Numerical Variables
When both variables are numeric, the objective is to examine whether a relationship exists between the two variables.
For example, application login frequency and monthly transaction count may be related if customers who interact with the application more frequently also perform more transactions.
Scatter plots are used to visualise such relationships.


Show the code
ggplot(df,
       aes(x = app_logins_frequency,
           y = avg_daily_transactions))+
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth()











5 Categorical vs Categorical Variables
When both variables are categorical, the goal is to examine whether there is an association between the categories.
For example, the relationship between income bracket and preferred transaction type may reveal whether customers with different income levels prefer different transaction behaviours.
Bar charts and mosaic plots will be used to visualise such relationships.

Bar ChartMosaic Plot




Show the code
ggplot(df,
       aes(x = income_bracket,
           fill = preferred_transaction_type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(y = "Proportion")













Show the code
ggplot(data = df) +
  geom_mosaic(
    aes(x = product(income_bracket),
        fill = preferred_transaction_type)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Income Bracket and Preferred Transaction Type",
    x = "Income Bracket",
    y = "Proportion"
  )














6 Statistical Validity
For each of the visualisation options described above, statistical validity tests can be performed, by selecting the type of test (parametric/non parametric) and the confidence interval.
Based on the type of variables analysed, the different plots are shown.

Categorical vs NumericalNumerical vs NumericalCategorical vs Categorical




Show the code
ggbetweenstats(            
  data = df,
  x = income_bracket,
  y = avg_tx_value,
  type = "nonparametric",  
  conf.level = 0.99        
)













Show the code
ggscatterstats(
  data = df,
  x = app_logins_frequency,
  y = avg_daily_transactions,
  marginal = FALSE
)













Show the code
ggbarstats(
  data = df,
  x = income_bracket,
  y = preferred_transaction_type,
  conf.level = 0.99
)














7 Multivariate Analysis
To visualise the relationship between more than two variables, correlation plots can be used.


Show the code
selected_data <- df[, c("age", "household_size", "active_products", "app_logins_frequency", "feature_usage_diversity"), drop = FALSE]

corr_matrix <- cor(selected_data, method = "pearson", use = "complete.obs")

corrplot(corr_matrix, method = "ellipse",
type = "full",
order = "original",
diag = TRUE,
addCoef.col = "black",
tl.col = "black",
tl.srt = 90,
col = colorRampPalette(c("#b2182b", "white", "#2166ac"))(200) )

title: Data Preparation
text:
This app utilises the COFINFAD: Colombian Fintech Financial Analytics Dataset, which consists of two primary data files: customer_data.csv and transactions_data.csv. These datasets are linked through a common identifier, “customer_id”. The data will be imported into R using the read_csv() function from the readr package.
The customer.csv dataset will serve as the primary dataset for this project. Each row represents an individual customer, while each column captures different aspects of the customer’s profile and behaviour. The dataset provides a comprehensive view across multiple dimensions, including:

Demographic characteristics (e.g., age, gender, location, income bracket, education level, marital status)
Financial product ownership (e.g., savings accounts, credit cards, loans, investment and insurance products)
Digital engagement metrics (e.g., app login frequency, feature usage)
Aggregated transaction behaviour (e.g., number of transactions, average transaction value, total transaction volume, transaction frequency)
Customer experience indicators (e.g., satisfaction scores, app ratings)

Three variables contain missing data. The variable credit_utilization_ratio contains 18,263 missing values, which corresponds to customers who do not hold a credit card and therefore do not have a recorded utilization ratio. Additionally, feature_requests contains 16,115 missing values and complaint_topics contains 24,346 missing values. These missing values are expected, as not all customers provide feature requests or submit complaints. Since these missing values reflect the absence of feedback rather than data errors, they will be retained in the dataset for analysis.

title: Data Preparation
text:
3.2 Checking for Duplicates
To ensure that each observation represents a unique customer, the dataset is checked for duplicate values in the customer_id variable. This is done using the duplicated() function in R to identify whether any customer IDs appear more than once. The results show that there are no duplicate customer_id values in the dataset, confirming that each row corresponds to a unique customer record.

sum(duplicated(df$customer_id))

[1] 0

title: Data Preparation
text:
3.3 Converting Variables
Some variables in the dataset are converted to more appropriate data types to ensure they are handled correctly during analysis. Several categorical variables are originally stored as character variables and are converted to factor variables so that they are treated as categorical data rather than plain text. These variables include gender, income_bracket, occupation, education_level, marital_status, acquisition_channel, customer_segment, feedback_sentiment, clv_segment, and preferred_transaction_type. Converting these variables to factors allows them to be used more effectively in grouping, summarisation, and statistical modelling.
In addition, the variable customer_id is converted from numeric to character format. Since this variable serves only as a unique identifier for each customer and is not used in numerical calculations, converting it to a character variable prevents it from being mistakenly treated as a quantitative variable during analysis.

df$customer_id <- as.character(df$customer_id)

df$gender <- as.factor(df$gender)
df$income_bracket <- as.factor(df$income_bracket)
df$occupation <- as.factor(df$occupation)
df$education_level <- as.factor(df$education_level)

Note



The data set contains two sets of transaction metrics. The variables avg_tx_value, total_tx_volume, first_tx, last_tx represent aggregated transaction behaviour derived from the transaction dataset. A second set of transaction-related variables (average_transaction_value, total_transaction_volume, first_transaction_date, last_transaction_date) appears to represent derived behavioural metrics and will not be used in the analysis to avoid duplication. Additionally, transaction_frequency and avg_daily_transactions both calculate the average number of transactions per day, hence only avg_daily_transactions will be used for analysis.


Finally, the cleaned data set is stored as “cleaned_data.csv”, which is used for the further analysis.
